source_refs.note: Book p. 284: 14.4.1 introduction, (a) scalar and (b) vector triple product, definition of the scalar triple product, three cyclic forms, notation [u v w]. Book error: closing bracket missing. Teaching notes, Key points, mistakes are ours.

blocks.text: The scalar triple product is a key concept in vector calculus, with wide-ranging applications in various fields. In three-dimensional space it plays a significant role in calculating the volume of geometric shapes such as parallelepipeds and tetrahedrons defined by three vectors, which we will learn later in this chapter. It is also a vital tool for determining the coplanarity of vectors: it gives a condition to verify whether three vectors lie within the same plane.
There are two types of triple product of vectors:
In this section we shall study the scalar triple product only.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Look at the last operation in each product. In (a) the last operation is a dot product, so the answer is a number (scalar). In (b) the last operation is a cross product, so the answer is a vector. That is where the two names come from. The vector triple product is not part of this section.

The scalar triple product \(\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}\) is written as

blocks.text_alt: u dot (v cross w) equals the box product u v w

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book prints the product without its closing bracket, as "u · (v × w". It should read \(\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
Why is the answer a number? \(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}\) is a vector; the dot product of \(\underline{u}\) with that vector is a number.
The order of the operations is fixed: first the cross product, then the dot product. The other grouping \((\underline{u}\cdot \underline{v})\times \underline{w}\) has no meaning, because \(\underline{u}\cdot \underline{v}\) is a number and a cross product needs two vectors. For this reason the brackets are often dropped: \(\underline{u}\cdot \underline{v}\times \underline{w}\) always means \(\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\). The book writes it this way in Examples 24 and 25.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text:
The three forms in the definition keep the cyclic order \(\underline{u} \to \underline{v} \to \underline{w} \to \underline{u}\): each one is the previous one with the letters moved one place round the circle. All three give the same number; 14.4.2 shows why with volumes and 14.4.4 with determinants.
If you swap two of the vectors (break the cyclic order) the sign changes, because \(\underline{w}\times \underline{v} = -(\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\):
\[\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{w}\times \underline{v}) = -\,\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\]
In the box notation \([\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\) the vectors are listed in the order in which they appear in \(\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\).

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. Two triple products: scalar \(\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\) (a number) and vector \(\underline{u}\times(\underline{v}\times \underline{w})\) (a vector).
2. Scalar triple product: first \(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}\), then the dot product with \(\underline{u}\).
3. Notation: \(\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}) = [\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\).
4. Cyclic forms are equal: \(\underline{u}\cdot(\underline{v}\times \underline{w}) = \underline{v}\cdot(\underline{w}\times \underline{u}) = \underline{w}\cdot(\underline{u}\times \underline{v})\).
5. Swapping two vectors changes the sign.

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Doing the dot product first: \((\underline{u}\cdot \underline{v})\times \underline{w}\) is meaningless.
2. Writing the answer as a vector, e.g. with \(\underline{i}, \underline{j}, \underline{k}\): the scalar triple product is a number.
3. Changing the order of the vectors carelessly: \([\underline{u}\ \underline{w}\ \underline{v}] = -[\underline{u}\ \underline{v}\ \underline{w}]\), not equal to it.
